title: ch- at the start
text: The same two letters make three sounds, and the sound tells you the route a word took. Greek words say k (chorus, chaos, character). French words borrowed in the Middle Ages say ch (change, chief, chair), while later French loans say sh (chef, chic, champagne). Native words say ch too (child, choose).

title: ph anywhere
text: Latin writers spelled the Greek letter phi as ph, and English kept the habit. A ph almost always means the word is Greek underneath: phone, photo, philosophy, alphabet.

title: eau anywhere
text: Three vowels, one sound. eau is French spelling for an o sound: beau, bureau, plateau. Beautiful hides it in plain sight.

title: ps- at the start
text: Greek allowed words to begin with ps; English does not pronounce it, so the p goes silent: psychology, psalm, pseudonym.

title: pt- at the start
text: Another Greek opening English cannot say. pteron means wing, so pterodactyl is a wing-finger and the -pter in helicopter is the same wing.

title: rh- at the start
text: Greek marked a breathy r at the start of words, which Latin wrote as rh: rhythm, rhyme, rhinoceros, rhetoric.

title: sk- at the start
text: Old English turned sk into sh, so its own words say ship and shirt. Words that kept a hard sk were often borrowed from Old Norse: sky, skin, skirt, skull.

title: kn- at the start
text: The k used to be pronounced. Old English said knight with a k, and the spelling stayed after the sound dropped out around the 1600s: knee, knife, knock.

title: gh anywhere
text: gh stands for a throaty sound Old English had and modern English lost, like the ch in Scottish loch. That is why night, though and daughter carry letters nobody says.

title: -tion at the end
text: Latin made nouns from verbs with -tio, and French passed them on as -tion: nation, action, education. Tens of thousands of English words end this way.

title: -ology at the end
text: From Greek logia, the study of something. Biology is the study of life, geology of the earth, and almost every word ending -ology is built from Greek parts.

title: -ette at the end
text: A French ending that makes things small: kitchenette, cigarette, statuette. It is still productive, which is why English keeps inventing new ones.

title: -que at the end
text: A French spelling for a k sound at the end of a word: unique, antique, technique, boutique.

title: -o at the end
text: Native English words rarely end in o. Many that do came from Italian or Spanish: piano, tornado, potato, mosquito, volcano.
